hero.title: Overgrown front beds, **rebuilt from scratch.**
hero.lede: Grand Scapes rebuilds Burton landscapes that have outgrown the house: old shrubs and brick borders out, beds reshaped, new plants, fabric and mulch in, and the edges cut clean.

local.title: Why older Burton beds need a full rebuild.
local.intro: Many Burton homes went up in the 1960s, and the shrubs in front of them often went in at the same time. By now those shrubs cover the windows, and the old brick or timber borders have heaved and sunk. A rebuild starts with deciding what is worth keeping.

points.title: Old roots close to the house
points.body: Shrubs that sat against a foundation for decades leave big root balls. We dig them out with a compact track loader where there is room and by hand where there is not, and the bed gets fresh soil before anything new goes in.

points.title: Beds that drain away from the house
points.body: Most of Burton sits on soil that drains slowly. A rebuilt bed should pitch away from the house, with plants that need drier roots on the high side. If a whole corner stays wet, ask Rob about [grading](/grading-and-new-lawns/).

points.title: Filled ground on the west side
points.body: On the west side, toward Flint, much of the ground was cut and filled when the neighborhoods went in. What sits under a bed there varies from yard to yard, so we check the soil before choosing plants.

points.title: Salt on the street side
points.body: MSU Extension lists yews, roses, rhododendrons and white pines among the plants hurt by salt that builds up beside walks and drives. A bed along a Burton sidewalk or driveway does better with tougher plants up front.

logistics.title: How a Burton landscape job runs.
body: Rob meets you at the house, walks the beds and tells you what he would pull, what he would keep and what the yard needs. You get a price before any work starts, and nothing extra happens without your okay.

Demolition comes first: old shrubs, roots, borders and tired rock or mulch come out and leave in our dump trailer. Then the beds get shaped, fabric goes down, new plants go in, and the edge is finished in gray block or a clean cut natural edge, with black, brown or red mulch on top.

How long it takes depends on the size of the yard and the weather, and Rob lays out the plan at the estimate. To keep the new beds sharp afterward, [landscape maintenance](/landscape-maintenance/) and [mulch work in Burton](/mulch-installation-burton-mi/) pick up from there.

faq.q: Do you do landscaping in Burton, MI?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes rebuilds landscapes in Burton: old shrubs and small trees out, beds reshaped, new plants, fabric and mulch in, and new block or natural edges. The estimate is free, and Rob suggests what to do once he has seen the yard.

faq.q: Can you take out the overgrown bushes in front of my house?
faq.a: Yes. We dig out old bushes, roots and all, and small trees like an old cherry, then haul everything away. Big tree removal is not something we do. See [bush removal](/bush-removal/) for how that part goes.

faq.q: What should I plant next to a salted driveway?
faq.a: Plants that can take salt. MSU Extension says salt damages plants through spray and through buildup in the soil next to walks and drives, and it names yews, roses, rhododendrons and white pines as sensitive. Rob can suggest hardier choices for the street side of the bed.

faq.q: Why does water sit in my flower beds?
faq.a: Usually the ground drains slowly and the bed is shaped the wrong way. Burton loam is slow to drain, and the low spots are wetter still, so a bed that slopes toward the house or sits below the lawn will hold water. Regrading the bed away from the foundation is where we start.
